articles.title: Why Can You Click the Invisible Part of an SVG Icon?
articles.excerpt: Click just to the right of a half-visible SVG eye icon. The browser can still target the eye’s path, even though there’s nothing visible at that point. Swap the alpha mask for a clipPath, click the sa…
articles.body: Click just to the right of a half-visible SVG eye icon. The browser can still target the eye’s path, even though there’s nothing visible at that point. Swap the alpha mask for a clipPath , click the same spot again, and the button behind the SVG gets the click. That difference is easy to miss when reviewing an icon from a screenshot. Here’s a small test that makes it visible. Same path, same points Both panels use the same filled SVG path in a 160 × 120 viewBox. Each effect reveals only the left half. A button sits beneath each SVG so there’s a second target when the path misses. The dashed outline and point markers are on a separate overlay with pointer-events: none . A (22, 60) sits on the visible half of the eye. B (138, 60) sits on the hidden half of the original path.

articles.title: Before You Build It, Find the Handoff
articles.excerpt: If you build internal tools, integrations or automations for a business, you've probably been handed a ticket like this: "We need a new system for X." This Thanksgiving week we've been looking back at…
articles.body: If you build internal tools, integrations or automations for a business, you've probably been handed a ticket like this: "We need a new system for X." This Thanksgiving week we've been looking back at what our clients taught us in 2026. The short version: the most useful work we did often involved writing less code than the ticket asked for. Here are five lessons, written for the people who usually get asked to build. 1. Find the handoff, not the slow step Slow steps are visible, so they get the attention. The expensive problems tend to live in handoffs: the point where work moves from one person, team or system to the next. Handoffs are where data gets re-typed, exported to CSV, pasted into a second screen or "just checked" by someone. Nobody owns them, so nobody fixes them.

articles.body: A new physics benchmark was almost obsolete before researchers could publish it. GPT-6 Astra solved 49 of 50 unpublished problems, raising a difficult question for science: what should researchers test when artificial intelligence can already handle the calculations designed to measure its reasoning? Imagine a physicist arriving at a desk with a problem that has no familiar textbook solution. The task demands several pages of algebra, careful physical assumptions and enough judgment to notice when a result looks wrong. By the end of the day, the researcher may have a solution, or may discover that the problem itself contains a hidden complication. Now imagine assigning the same work to an AI agent in the morning and receiving solutions before lunch.

articles.title: We ran a company on an append-only ledger for 66 days. Here is the audit.
articles.excerpt: 12,873 events. 868 closed tasks. Zero revenue. A few things we got right, and one seam we chose not to hide. Most "AI agent" posts show you the happy path: a prompt, a plan, a pull request. This one i…
articles.body: 12,873 events. 868 closed tasks. Zero revenue. A few things we got right, and one seam we chose not to hide. Most "AI agent" posts show you the happy path: a prompt, a plan, a pull request. This one is the audit trail — including the part where the audit fails. For the last 66 days we've run a one-person company where the work is done by agents and every action lands in a single append-only ledger. Not a task board. Not a Notion database. One JSONL file, one writer, one hash per event. Here's what actually happened, what the mechanisms caught, and what they couldn't. The shape of the thing Two roles produce value: Builder — ships products, code, content, experiments. Seller — finds people, builds trust, collects money.

articles.title: Watch live: Europe unveils 1st close-up views of asteroid Dimorphos after NASA's DART impact
articles.excerpt: ESA will share the Hera probe's first images of asteroid Dimorphos today following NASA's historic DART mission that impacted the space rock two years ago.
articles.body: After a two-year journey, the Hera spacecraft is arriving at the Didymos double asteroid system, and its first images are being released to the public today (Nov. 25). The European Space Agency's (ESA's ) Hera probe launched atop a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Oct. 7, 2024 . Its destination is the Didymos-Dimorphos asteroid system, which consists of the larger Didymos , a " rubble pile" asteroid , and its smaller moonlet Dimorphos. NASA slammed a kinetic impactor into Dimorphos in 2022 in the historic DART test , which confirmed that such an impact can alter the trajectory of an asteroid. Hera arrives at Didymos today, and ESA is sharing the first close-up images from the mission in a free online livestream. ESA's livestream starts at 1:45 p.m.

articles.title: Astronomers discover the most distant and ancient supermassive black hole-powered quasar in the universe
articles.excerpt: The Euclid space telescope has spotted the most distant and ancient quasar ever seen, a bright cosmic event powered by a supermassive black hole with 360 million times the mass of the sun.
articles.body: The Euclid space telescope has spotted the most distant and ancient quasar ever seen, a bright cosmic event powered by a supermassive black hole with 360 million times the mass of the sun. The supermassive black hole is seen as it was just 630 million years after the Big Bang. 40 million years further back in time than the previous record holder for the most ancient quasar. The discovery further deepens the mystery of how supermassive black holes grew so massive so soon into the history of the universe. That's because previously, scientists had theorized it should take 1 billion years of feeding and merging for black holes to reach supermassive status of millions or billions of times as massive as the sun.

articles.title: November's full moon dazzles skywatchers with a stunning Beaver Moon supermoon (photos)
articles.excerpt: From the skyscrapers of New York to the ancient Parthenon in Athens, the Beaver Moon supermoon put on a spectacular show for skywatchers around the world.
articles.body: The November full moon rose to put on a spectacular natural light show on Nov. 24 and we've got the photos to prove it! Read on to see our favorite shots of the "Beaver Moon" captured from around the world. Each monthly full moon has its own set of informal names , often bestowed to reflect events occurring in the world at the time of their rising. The November moon is often known as the Beaver Moon, a name associated with the time of year when beavers prepare for winter and when trappers historically set beaver traps before waterways froze. November's full moon served as the opening salvo in a series of four dazzling supermoons , which turn full around the time that the natural satellite passes closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit.
